plan.topic: Compounded tirzepatide recall: Houston RX recalled 64 vials (Class II, lack of sterility assurance, started Sep 25, 2026) after an FDA inspection with 14 observations
plan.angle: Calm 'what's confirmed?' Short. Per the FDA enforcement report (cite the entry and its report date), Houston RX LLC, a Texas compounding pharmacy, recalled 64 vials of compounded tirzepatide-niacinamide, Class II, for lack of assurance of sterility, initiated Sep 25, 2026 (confirm against the FDA record). An FDA inspection on Aug 20–28, 2026 listed 14 observations (FDA Form 483). One line: anything injected has to be sterile. Compounded drugs aren't FDA-approved or reviewed; branded tirzepatide is FDA-approved. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist what product you're on and about FDA-approved options. Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own. Prescriber line. Follow for more. No emoji, 170 words or fewer.

plan.why: Our strongest Short lane (gray-market 'what's confirmed?' Shorts: median 103.5) with a new fact: mainstream recall coverage peaked on Oct 19. | fact-check: Mostly confirmed. FDA enforcement-report data relayed by Medical Daily and others: Houston RX LLC (a 503A pharmacy) recalled 64 vials, Class II, for lack of assurance of sterility, initiated Sep 25, 2026. The FDA Form 483 (fda.gov/media/195122) covers an inspection on Aug 20–28, 2026 with 14 observations. Corrections and risks: (1) The recalled product is compounded tirzepatide-NIACINAMIDE 20 mg/2 mg per mL vials, not plain tirzepatide. The title and narration must say 'compounded tirzepatide-niacinamide vials' or 'a compounded tirzepatide combination', or the claim is wrong. (2) One secondary site gives the initiation date as Sep 10. The scriptwriter must confirm the date, class, quantity and reason against the FDA Enforcement Report entry itself and cite that entry with its report date. If the entry can't be retrieved, cite only the 483 and leave out the date. (3) Keep to what was confirmed: one pharmacy and 64 vials. The FDA has not reported injuries in the sources found, so don't imply harm or widespread contamination, and don't list graphic or alarming 483 details (exposed skin, microbial growth) beyond one calm line. Naming the recalling firm, credited to the FDA record, is acceptable. Name no other pharmacy, telehealth or seller. (4) Say compounded drugs are not FDA-approved and not FDA-reviewed for safety, effectiveness or quality, and that branded tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) is FDA-approved, without making it sound like an ad. Title: drop dosing details. 'Compounded Tirzepatide Recall: What the FDA Confirmed (Oct 2026)' is fine if the body says 'tirzepatide-niacinamide'.

script.hook_pattern: The hook pairs recognition with a curiosity gap ("Saw the headlines? Here's what's actually confirmed") in a calm "What's Actually Confirmed?" voice. It names compounded tirzepatide and the word "recall" in the first second. Scene 2 names the worry and says it's fair. Every fact is credited to an FDA record or to Medical Daily's report of it. Re-hooks land at about 15 s ("here's why it matters") and about 30 s ("the part most people miss"). The ending gives the viewer something to do (ask your prescriber or pharmacist), then the prescriber line and a follow ask. No long-form is named because no related long-form is live. Production notes: (1) No emoji anywhere. (2) The initiation date stays out of the script. (3) Captions must show the numerals "64", "14", "Class II" and "type 2", never number words. (4) No sound effects under "sixty-four", "fourteen", "tirzepatide-niacinamide" or "Houston R X". (5) Masking must be 0.03 or lower. (6) src2 is the URL Medical Daily links as the Houston RX 483. Open the PDF and check that the cover page says Houston RX LLC, Aug 20–28, 2026, before upload. (7) s5 source note: the final sentence ("anything injected has to be sterile") is general context, not attributed to src2/src6. If an on-screen sterility line is added there, it gets no source tag. (8) Scene 1 on-screen text says "Compounded" so viewers watching muted don't read it as a recall of branded tirzepatide. (9) Spoken word count: 167.

factcheck.summary: The Short is accurate and safe, and can ship after the small fixes listed below. Medical Daily's report (Oct 19, 2026) backs every claim about the recall. It confirms that Houston RX LLC in North Houston recalled 64 two-millilitre vials of compounded tirzepatide-niacinamide (20 mg/2 mg per mL). It was a Class II recall for "lack of assurance of sterility", and the recall started Sep 25, 2026. An FDA inspection on Aug 20–28, 2026 ended with a Form 483 listing 14 observations. Medical Daily links that 483 to fda.gov/media/195122/download. The link works and returns a PDF, but the PDF wouldn't parse here, so I couldn't read the firm name myself. FDA's 'Concerns with Unapproved GLP-1 Drugs' page (updated 10/01/2026) says word for word: "Compounded drugs are not FDA approved... the agency does not review compounded drugs for safety, effectiveness or quality." FDA pages confirm Mounjaro's approval (May 13, 2022, blood sugar control in adults with type 2 diabetes) and Zepbound's (Nov 8, 2023, chronic weight management). The safety lines are all present: no switching, stopping or changing medicines on your own, and the prescriber line points to FDA-approved options. No compounded or online seller is promoted, the scope is pinned to one pharmacy, and the title pays off. I couldn't pull the record from FDA's Enforcement Report database myself; it only takes searches on its own site, and my web search didn't turn it up. The only fixes are to source labels, a production note and one optional wording tweak.
